question: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems play an essential role in supporting improved glycaemic control, health outcomes, patient education and self-management. As more CGM systems are entering the EU market, clinicians and people living with diabetes have raised concerns about device quality, limited transparency in clinical performance evaluation, and the lack of comparable data on real-world performance.
This raises questions about whether notified bodies and regulatory authorities have the tools needed to ensure patient safety and trust in line with the highest performance standards. 1.

Starting from 28 May 2026, EUDAMED will provide digital information on the life cycle of medical devices. However it remains limited in scope, especially for medium to high-risk devices. How does the Commission intend to ensure that healthcare professionals and people living with diabetes can meaningfully benefit from access to transparent, comparable and clinically relevant performance data – including on accuracy, testing conditions and system alignment – to support informed clinical decision-making?
Does the Commission intend to establish common specifications for CGM systems, taking into account stakeholder input?
answer: Continuous glucose monitoring systems (CGMs) in the scope of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical device s (1) (MDR) or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (2) (IVDR) on the EU market must comply with the general safety and performance requirements laid down in these Regulations and undergo the relevant conformity assessment procedures, quality and risk management, and clinical studies, to ensure a high level of protection of health and safety of patients.

The European database on medical devices (3) provides information to professionals and patients on devices of all classes placed on the EU market, including CGMs, as a major tool for transparency. The first four modules became mandatory to use as of 28 May 2026 (4), while the module on Clinical Investigations and Performance Studies is under development.

For CGMs, adding to harmonised standards already available for quality management system s (5), risk management (6) and blood-glucose monitoring systems (7), the Commission is collecting information from stakeholders to update its request to the European standardisation organisations (8) to adopt new harmonised standards for CGMs.

In parallel, to provide for a short-term solution, the Commission has raised to the Medical Device Coordination Group the intention to develop device-specific guidance to clarify the implementation of certain requirements and technical solutions for CGMs.

The development of harmonised standards and of common specifications for the requirements to be met by CGMs in accordance with MDR/IVDR Article 9, would require a longer timeframe. The Commission is thus considering acting at both levels, proposing guidance and initiating the process for standards and/or common specifications, as necessary.
